::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Why can you add $-a$ to both sides of $a+b=a+c$?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3337381/why-can-you-add-a-to-both-sides-of-ab-ac), asked by [Ion Aag](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/699246/ion-aag) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2019-08-28; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> ```
>  We are given that a+b = a+c
>
>
>    (-a) + (a+b) = (-a) + (a+c) 
>
>    ((-a)+a) + b = ((-a)+a) + c           by BR2
>
>    (a+(-a)) + b = (a+(-a)) + c           by BR1
>
>             0+b = 0+c                    by BR4
>
> 	  b = c                      by BR1 and BR3
> ```
>
>
>
> How is (-a) added? Where does that come from? How is that step allowed/legal?
:::

This is one of the “Axioms” or common notions written in Euclid's *Elements.*  The [complete list](https://mathcs.clarku.edu/~djoyce/java/elements/bookI/cn.html) is:

> 1. Things which equal the same thing also equal one another.
> 2. If equals are added to equals, then the wholes are equal.
> 3. If equals are subtracted from equals, then the remainders are equal.
> 4. Things which coincide with one another equal one another.
> 5. The whole is greater than the part.

Your derivation uses Axiom 3.  Now that we understand subtraction as just another form of addition (by negative numbers), Axioms 2 and 3 are considered equivalent.
